text: You get the root of a binary tree. Return its maximum depth — the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — we count nodes, not edges. So a single node is depth one, and an empty tree is depth zero. Is that right?
Correct. Nodes, and empty is zero.

Good. Then here is the thing I want to say up front, because it shapes the whole solution. The depth of the subtree under a node only depends on its two children, not on anything above it. So no information has to travel down the tree. Every number is born at the bottom, at the empty spots, and grows on the way back up. That means I don't need to pass a level or a counter into the call — the return value carries everything. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to about ten to the fourth nodes. Values are ints, and the tree can be any shape.

Any shape is worth noting. Ten thousand nodes can be one long chain, so recursion depth can hit ten thousand. That's fine for a normal stack, but I'll mention it later. Let me run through the example: three, nine, twenty, null, null, fifteen, seven. Nine is a leaf, so the left side gives depth one. Twenty has two leaves, so the right side gives depth two. The root adds one on top of the bigger one, so the answer is three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to list every root-to-leaf path, measure each one, and take the longest. That works, but it stores paths I never need — the number of leaves can be linear in n. This problem reminds me of a plain post-order DFS, the solve the children first, then combine shape. It fits because the answer at a node is a pure function of the two child answers. BFS by levels is the other option. It also gives the right answer, but its queue can hold about half the nodes at the widest level. I'll go with recursion because the code is two lines and the combine step is obvious. If the tree could be very deep, BFS would be the safer pick.

Here's the plan. One: an empty subtree returns zero. Two: otherwise, recurse into both children. Three: return one plus the bigger of the two. One thing worth flagging — the base case has to return zero, not one. If it returns one, every answer comes out exactly one too big — not one per level. The reason is that max is transparent to a shared offset: one plus the max of a plus one and b plus one equals one plus the max of a and b, plus one. The extra one rides along instead of piling up. Over every tree shape up to seven nodes, the error was plus one every time. There's a trade-off here. Recursion uses a call stack as deep as the tree; BFS doesn't. For this input size recursion is fine. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The null check returns zero, and the second line is one plus the max of the two recursive calls. One thing worth flagging — max here is an ordinary function, not a short-circuit operator like double-ampersand. Both arguments are evaluated before max runs, so both recursive calls always happen; no side is ever skipped. That's why the work is completely predictable: one call per node plus one per empty slot, and a tree with n nodes has n plus one empty slots. So it's exactly two n plus one calls, whatever the shape.

Let's dry-run the code with the same example, and I expect three. The returns finish bottom-up. The only row where max makes a real choice is the root: it sees one on the left and two on the right, throws the left away, and returns three. Everywhere else the two sides tie. Eleven calls, matching two n plus one with n equal to five. Corner cases: an empty tree hits the guard and returns zero. A single node is one plus the max of zero and zero, which is one. A left-going chain of five nodes gives five. And if I swap max for plus, it still compiles but silently counts nodes instead.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: every node is visited once with constant work, and the exact call count is two n plus one. Space is order h for the call stack. In the worst-case scenario the tree is one long chain, so h equals n and the stack is linear; on a balanced tree it's logarithmic. Oh, one more thing — since the call count doesn't depend on shape, the running time is fully determined by n. Shape only changes the stack depth, never the number of calls, and that's a direct result of max not short-circuiting.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You said up front that nothing flows downward and all the values are born at the null base case, which is the real structure of the problem. You explained why a wrong base case is a constant off-by-one instead of a compounding one, and backed it with the algebra of max. And you pointed out that max does not short-circuit, so the call count is exactly two n plus one, no matter the shape. Good work.
